title: The second bell of Muileann naomh holds
summary: After the first bell cast for the hawk-house at Muileann naomh cracks in its first frost, the founders cast a second, thicker at the waist, and it holds, ringing thereafter at every measured burning kept at the house and at every turn of the coast's own reckoning of the year besides.

title: Cuan dhearg rebuilds a street back from the shore
summary: After An Gàire Dubh drowns its waterfront, Cuan dhearg of the red cliffs rebuilds a full street back from the old shoreline, on ground no telling the town keeps says the sea has ever reached, and the new street holds.

title: King Tormod visits Cuan dhearg's new street
summary: King Tormod Bàn rides to Cuan dhearg to see its rebuilt street, the one journey of his reign made, his own scribes note, for a storm's sake alone rather than for a war, a crowning or a rite the crown was bound to keep.

title: A reciter of Clann na Ceiste says the Mason's line at a naming
summary: At a naming among the wells of Tobar dhìreach, for a steward's son of the king's own household, the reciter Muireach mac Ailein says the line of the Mason over the child rather than the long line of Somhairle that royal namings there have called on for generations.

title: Birth of Catrìona nic Aonghais at Inis thais
summary: A daughter, Catrìona, is born at Inis thais to Aonghas mac Iain, the king's brother, and his wife Mairead nic Ailein, the first child of that marriage to live past her own naming. King Tormod Bàn rides down himself to see her named.

title: Muileann naomh draws pilgrims from further south
summary: Word of the hawk-house at Muileann naomh, where the old teaching is still given whole and unsoftened, carries south along the coast, and pilgrims begin to come to it from towns further south than any hawk-house had drawn from before.

title: Death of Aonghas mac Iain
summary: Aonghas mac Iain, the king's brother, dies at Inis thais in his fifty-fourth year of a wasting sickness, King Tormod Bàn having ridden down to sit with him three days before the end. He is buried in the ground of that coast, at his own household's asking.

title: Mairead nic Ailein keeps her daughter from the red hall
summary: Offered a place under the king's own roof for her widowed household, Mairead nic Ailein keeps her daughter Catrìona at Inis thais rather than raise her at Cathair dhearg, judging a fatherless girl better raised among neighbours than as a king's ward with an unnamed claim.

title: Iain Odhar cleared of blame for the ferry
summary: The ferryman Iain Odhar comes before the king's reeves to answer for the ferry's overturning, and is cleared: he judged the spate as he had judged the river a hundred times before, and no such flood had come down that crossing unwarned in his eleven years on the rope.

title: A new ferry ordered a mile upstream
summary: King Tormod Bàn has the old ferry rope cut and burned and orders a second crossing built a mile upstream, where the ford-keepers judge the river safer in spate, and never crosses the Abhainn fhionn again without a rider sent ahead to test the current.

title: Iain Odhar made keeper of the new crossing
summary: The king grants Iain Odhar a small holding above the new crossing, not as payment for the two lives the old ferry took, but as a keeper's fee, and the ferryman watches the new rope closely for the thirty years he has left to keep it.

title: Raghnall Ruadh made master of the vein-house
summary: The custodians of the vein-house at Muileann dhearg choose Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill, as master over two men of longer service, judging that a vein-house that may soon answer to no clear crown had better answer to the steadiest hand at hand.

title: A councillor asks King Tormod to name an heir
summary: An old councillor of the red hall asks King Tormod Bàn, seven years after the ferry, whether he means to name one of the three standing nearest the crown before age chooses in his place. The king answers that he will hold the crown himself while breath allows it.

title: The houses hold the hall in common
summary: Unable to agree on any one of the three claims laid before them, the seven houses hold the red hall in common, a council of custodians sitting in the crown's stead and keeping the kingdom's small business moving while the larger question of the crown stands unanswered.

title: Tormod Bàn hears the tidings of An Gàire Dubh standing
summary: Word of the sea driven over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg reaches the red hall nine days late by a rider who has ridden two horses to death. King Tormod Bàn, nine-and-fifty, hears it standing, as his scribes note he does only when a report troubles him past sitting.

title: The king sends grain south unasked
summary: Before the roads close for the winter King Tormod Bàn sends grain south to Cuan dhearg, though its reeve has sent no asking, only the bare report of the water; the season's salt fish had spoiled on the racks below the town.

title: The three nearest the crown reckoned
summary: In the fourth year after the ferry, the custodians of the vein-house cease to reckon quietly who stands nearest the crown: Dùghall Garbh the king's half-brother, Catrìona nic Aonghais his niece, and Raghnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill.

title: Tormod Bàn's last order
summary: Dying at Cathair dhearg at seven-and-eighty, one-and-fifty years crowned, King Tormod Bàn gives his last clear order to the scribe beside him: that the boundary dispute at Àth chiar, unsettled after three seasons, go to the custodians to finish.
